stories.topic: Black Death Pogroms and the 1933 Nazi Vote
stories.summary: Ajay opens with research on Germany. Cities where Jews were attacked in pogroms during the fourteenth-century Black Death, after being accused of bringing the plague, had a statistically higher Nazi vote share in the 1933 election. The finding came back to him on a recent trip to Pune.
stories.insight: Culture is sticky over centuries. A shock from nearly six hundred years ago can still show up in the data, so a city's present can be read as the residue of its deep past.
stories.quote: So across hundreds of years there is stickiness in culture.

stories.topic: Pune's Endowment, and Twenty Pages of Criticism
stories.summary: Pune feels like a mid-sized second-tier city today, but a scant two hundred years ago the Peshwas ran India's biggest empire from it, with finance ministers, military strategists and logistics experts. On a two-day visit Ajay met what he calls the height of Pune's intelligentsia. Among them were the Prayas Energy Group, co-founded by his late friend Girish Sant, and about ten manufacturing CEOs gathered by Prashant Girbane of the Maratha Chamber of Commerce. That meeting was devoted entirely to criticising EIE's two manufacturing episodes. Ajay sat and listened.
stories.insight: Being a capital is an initial endowment that keeps compounding: resources draw thinking, research and educational institutions for centuries. And the right response to informed criticism is delight, not defensiveness.
stories.quote: I took twenty pages of notes from people in the room criticizing our episodes. I was just so delighted, I was just so happy that I'm getting to meet people who actually know this better than us and who are criticizing us

stories.summary: The best feedback came from his IIT wingmate Ajay Bhagavat. Global competition makes it very hard for manufacturing to earn an operating profit margin above 15%. Early software and services firms earned 50 to 70%, and that margin paid for their learning curve. Manufacturing instead demands a 5, 10 or 15-year journey of learning its intricate complexity without making cash hand over fist.
stories.insight: Manufacturing is harder than services for a structural reason, not just a policy one. Thin margins mean there is no cushion for learning, so it takes an ethos of patience and a willingness to commit to 10 to 20-year journeys of excellence.
stories.quote: And that operating profit margin paid for a learning curve. Whereas here that operating profit margin is low.

stories.summary: Amit traces Pune's ferment to education as well as to the Peshwas. Gokhale and his colleagues founded the Deccan Education Society, which includes Amit's alma mater Fergusson College, and Gandhi first met Gokhale on its grounds in 1894. Gopal Ganesh Agarkar once asked a biology class what God would look like if donkeys had a God, then gestured to show it would be a donkey. In B.R. Nanda's biography of Gokhale, an Englishwoman hears that Gokhale teaches at Fergusson and exclaims about the place. Amit adds that Pune produced great liberals but also a deep RSS base, and Godse.
stories.insight: A genuine culture of ideas breeds radicalism in several directions at once. Nineteenth-century Pune was more irreverent than many places would tolerate today.
stories.quote: Oh, Fergusson, that hotbed of atheism.

stories.topic: How a Country With No Navy Won the Black Sea
stories.summary:
Early in the war, Ukraine's navy was one ship, which it scuttled so Russia couldn't capture it. Russia's fleet sat in Sevastopol, a great natural port and Russian base since the Crimean War of the mid-nineteenth century. Ukraine used three innovations:
1. Constant NATO-quality and drone surveillance, so every Russian ship's latitude and longitude was known in real time.
2. Shore-based anti-ship missiles skimming two metres above the waves, hidden in sea clutter on ship radar, which sank the Moskva.
3. Drone boats carrying a thousand kg of explosive, some steered via Starlink dishes. When Russian helicopters hunted them, the boats were redesigned to fire anti-air missiles back.
Russia stopped using Sevastopol, and Ukrainian commercial ships ply the Black Sea again.
stories.insight: The decisive weapon was a culture of engineering under fire. That means rejecting the 'third world' assumption that equipment is fixed for the duration of a war. Amit adds the incentive lens: for Ukraine the war is existential, so it must innovate.
stories.quote: I want to get an innovation out in the field next week.

stories.topic: The Hellscape of the Ukraine Front
stories.summary: Two exhausted armies face each other across something new in history. It is not a line of trenches one or two kilometres apart, as in the First World War, but a 10 to 30 km no-man's-land under relentless drone surveillance and precision-guided munitions. Anything that moves is seen. Massing 500 men and 50 tanks gets spotted and destroyed. Russia, nearly out of Soviet equipment, has resorted to golf carts. Soldiers huddle and hide, managing only small, dinky actions day after day.
stories.insight: Pervasive sensing plus cheap precision strike has made the battlefield itself uninhabitable. Amit notes that because technology drives the expansion, the hellscape could keep growing.
stories.quote: They will send one drone to kill one soldier.

stories.summary: Over 18 months, Ukrainian special forces smuggled materials into safe houses inside Russia, one right next to an FSB building, and assembled 117 attack drones with 3D printers. The drones went into shipping containers on trucks driven by unwitting commercial drivers, told to wait at a Google Maps pin 5 to 10 km from five air bases. By the time the trucks moved, every Ukrainian had left Russia. From Ukraine, a button opened the container roofs and the drones flew out. They ran on ordinary Russian mobile-data SIMs, reportedly streamed video over Telegram, and may have used onboard AI with a table of Russia's costliest planes. About 20 aircraft, central to the nightly bombing of Ukraine and worth an estimated $2 to 3 billion, were destroyed for about $0.5 million. Amit adds that the containers had false ceilings, so an inspecting cop would find nothing.
stories.insight: Commercial off-the-shelf technology now lets the weak strike deep inside the strong at an absurd cost ratio. A country's own interior is no longer safe ground.
stories.quote: And that just makes you think what else are they working on?

stories.summary: Mossad operatives built a safe house inside Iran, shipped in parts and 3D-printed drones. In a synchronised assault, those drones rose from inside Iran and knocked out much of its air defence just before Israeli planes arrived to hit targets across the country. Whether the nuclear programme was stopped is unknown; perhaps 400 kg of 60% enriched uranium remains. But Ajay says Iran's conventional power was set back five or ten years. Iran retaliated with probably 1,000 missiles and drones, and only about 50 got through.
stories.insight: Spider Web is a template, not a one-off: covert inside-out drone strikes combined with a conventional outside-in attack. Missile defence has also reached a new level.
stories.quote: So Israeli air defense is so great that essentially everything got killed in the sky.

stories.topic: The India-Pakistan Skirmish Fought From Home Airspace
stories.summary: Ajay first insists on terminology: by international standard a war needs 1,000 deaths, so this was a skirmish or conflict, not a war. In the four days, planes on both sides stayed high over their own territory and fired standoff weapons at each other. To fire deep into Pakistan, Indian planes had to climb, which made them visible to ground radars and exposed them to ground-to-air and air-to-air missiles.
stories.insight: The dogfight imagery of 1965 and 1971 is obsolete. Air combat now means beyond-visual-range exchanges in which neither side crosses the border.
stories.quote: I am standing on Indian soil, you are standing on Pakistani soil, and we are merrily shooting at each other and planes are getting down.

stories.topic: The First Hour of a War on Taiwan
stories.summary: Half the world's military experts study Ukraine; the other half war-game a Chinese invasion of Taiwan, which Xi Jinping has openly talked about. China is deeply infiltrated in Taiwan, with operatives inside and connections to the Taiwanese underworld, and containers flow constantly through this trading nation. Reading about Spider Web, Ajay feared the war's first hour would be fought from inside. Drones and operatives would take out political and military leadership and air defences, creating chaos before a conventional second wave.
stories.insight: Open, trade-heavy societies are especially exposed to the inside-out attack model, so defence planning has to start at home.
stories.quote: So the moment I read about Operation Spider Web, my hopes and prayers went to Taiwan.

stories.topic: The Strange Sand of the Sinai
stories.summary: In the 1973 Yom Kippur War, Israeli equipment in the Sinai malfunctioned because the sand had characteristics never seen before. Tank treads, tyres and, he believes, bridging gear were affected. Scientists from the Weizmann Institute came to the battlefield and experimented with the sand while the war was going on. They went home and redesigned the bridging gear, which Ajay credits for Israel's success in the Sinai. Amit's verdict: 'Human software.'
stories.insight: Winning militaries fold scientists and problem-solvers into live operations. This is the case for the brainy soldier over the brawny one.
stories.quote: scientists from the Weizmann Institute in Jerusalem came, sat there on the sand, did experiments with the sand, all while the war was going on

stories.topic: Vasili Arkhipov, the Man Who Said 'Hold On'
stories.summary: In October 1962, during the Cuban Missile Crisis, the Soviet submarine B-59, carrying nuclear torpedoes, came under attack off Cuba. Its captain believed the two countries were at war and wanted to fire. Launching required three sign-offs: the captain, the political officer and the first officer. The first officer, Vasili Arkhipov, warned that if they were wrong, a nuclear first strike could trigger world war. He used his veto, and the torpedo was never fired.
stories.insight: Amit uses this story to frame his first fear. Future wars will move at bewildering speed, and the incentive to delegate decisions to AI could erase the calm human checkpoint that saved the world in 1962.
stories.quote: the nuclear torpedo wasn't fired because of the processes you had in place because one man was able to sit down and take a calm decision.

recommendations.creator: David Petraeus & Andrew Roberts
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation at the end of the episode. He describes the authors as 'one a great historian, one a general and a very fine thinker' and expects Ajay would recommend it too.
recommendations.reason: A book on the recent history and evolution of warfare that Amit enjoyed a few months ago and found full of things he didn't know. He had wanted to use it as the base for a 'history of war' episode before Ajay steered them to the future.

recommendations.context: Amit's source for the anecdote of an Englishwoman calling Fergusson College 'that hotbed of atheism'.
recommendations.reason: A window into Gokhale and the radical intellectual culture of late-nineteenth-century Pune.

recommendations.reason: It had a section on the future of war, including Operation Spider Web's false-ceiling containers and the scenario of terrorists launching swarms of cheap drones.

recommendations.context: Mentioned at the start as covering some of what future war looks like, and again when Amit raises the problem of attributing attacks.
recommendations.reason: It explains why, in modern conflict, you may not know whether you've been attacked or by whom.

recommendations.context: Ajay's own article, discussed in the defence-economics section.

core_ideas.concept: You Can't Understand the State Without Understanding War
core_ideas.explanation: Early states really did one thing: wage war. Creating internal peace was relatively cheap. War is what forced states to build fiscal systems to raise money and to learn public procurement. War has repeatedly driven science and technology, and it shaped the very boundaries of states. Abhorring violence doesn't make war go away; you have to understand the world in order to play it well.
core_ideas.quote: A simple abhorrence of cruelty and violence doesn't put an end to war. A simple insistence on pacifism does not solve the problem of war.

core_ideas.concept: The Sword and the Shield: War Advances in Discontinuous Jumps
core_ideas.explanation: Military history is an endless dance between attack and defence, punctuated by technologies that suddenly make old force designs obsolete. Aircraft carriers made the Royal Navy's battleship fleet look wrong-footed when Japan destroyed British ships near Singapore. German tanks with Stuka dive-bomber support stunned Poland and France. Ajay argues the last five years are another such break, bigger than the Gulf War's 'first triumph of silicon over steel'.
core_ideas.quote: Sometimes development in the techniques of war favor the sword. So attackers get an upper hand. Sometimes they favor the shield.

core_ideas.explanation: Asked how he would revamp India's military, Ajay refuses to jump to a to-do list. He first lays out nine principles, then derives strategy from them.
core_ideas.quote: Great countries are not built out of getting shit done. Great countries are built out of thinking and principles and imagination and philosophy.

core_ideas.concept: The Intelligence Revolution Kills Surprise, Mass and the Safe Rear
core_ideas.explanation: Satellite imagery, drone imagery and open-source intelligence mean the enemy sees everything. If you mass forces for a breakthrough in the Second World War or Soviet deep-battle style, they are spotted and destroyed by precision weapons. Every major campaign in Ukraine has been fully known to the other side. Logistics suffers too: ammunition dumps and supply trucks are visible targets, and a logistics truck is now more prized than a tank.
core_ideas.quote: So principle one is that the old ways of surprise and mass are well and truly and firmly gone.

core_ideas.concept: Strategic War Is a War of Economies, and Burn Rates Have Exploded
core_ideas.explanation: Long wars are decided by production, innovation and the defence industrial base, because stored stocks run out. The intelligence revolution makes this worse. Israel's military has a system that fuses all its sensors into targeting data, producing targets at an unprecedented rate, so munitions are burned far faster than any peacetime factory supplies. Ajay's answer is to design surge capacity in advance. Private producers should run one shift in peacetime but be contractually ready to scale 3x to 5x on demand.
core_ideas.quote: So we need to build surge capabilities into ordinary peacetime defense procurement, rather than running around when a war comes.

core_ideas.explanation: At short range, defence now dominates: any attacking force is seen and destroyed before it can break through. At long range, attack dominates. Ukraine flies drones 1,000 to 2,000 km into Russia and destroys factories nightly, because ground-based air defences can be overwhelmed by volume. A factory in Dehradun was once safe during a war on the China border; now targets thousands of kilometres inside India are exposed.
core_ideas.quote: So it is very easy to kill a factory. It is very difficult to win a trench.

core_ideas.concept: The Soldier as Sensor, and the Algorithmic Fog of War
core_ideas.explanation: Modern soldiers spend much of their time reporting position, ammunition left and sightings into software. That data feeds situational-awareness systems which allocate scarce resources, like an 'Uber for artillery' matching a target to the best-placed gun. But too much data brings its own confusion, which Ajay calls the 'algorithmic fog of war', or death by data.
core_ideas.quote: As much as sending bullets out, the soldier is bringing information back. And information is power.

core_ideas.explanation: Upgrades once meant swapping hardware, stepping out of a Tiger tank into a King Tiger. Now every piece of equipment reduces to mobility, a sensor and a gun, and everything else is software. A new revision pushed over the air to a million devices at the front is an instant force upgrade. So wartime R&D that diagnoses problems day by day becomes a core combat capability.
core_ideas.quote: So there is some tank treads by which something moves, there are some sensors by which something sees, and there's a trigger by which something kills. The rest is all software.

core_ideas.explanation: The soldier of the future is less about machismo and fitness and more about intelligence and problem-solving on the fly. Ajay wants recruits who resemble teams inside India's technologically advanced private companies more than traditional junior-level military recruitment.
core_ideas.quote: Soldiers are not primarily about bravery, meaning, of course, they need to be brave. They are going to need to be innovative problem solvers faced with this new world and they will need to think on the fly and do problem solving and get good at it. They can't just obey orders.

core_ideas.concept: A Second World War-Speed Moment: Don't Fight the Last War
core_ideas.explanation: Between 1939 and Hiroshima, dogma was overturned every few months. Ajay believes we are in such a period now. Most militaries have only just digested 1967, 1973, Iraq and Afghanistan. The Russians, Chinese and Americans are all unprepared for what the last five years revealed, so experimentation and risk-taking are essential.
core_ideas.quote: So we need to do more of radical thinking, make mistakes, experiment, take risks.

core_ideas.concept: Ukraine Is Today's Spanish Civil War
core_ideas.explanation: Hitler perfected the Blitzkrieg in the Spanish Civil War of 1936, and the wise move for others was to be there and learn before Poland in 1939. Ukraine is today's live lab for conventional war between peers. Every sensible country should send teams there, which will likely mean helping Ukraine in return. Ukraine has also become a world-leading vendor of many weapons systems.
core_ideas.quote: Ukraine today is the global frontier. They know how to do this stuff. There is nobody who gets this like them.

core_ideas.concept: Nuclear Weapons Haven't Made Conventional War Obsolete
core_ideas.explanation: India, China and Pakistan once seemed locked in a nuclear standoff in which conventional war was a sideshow. Ajay argues conventional capability must go back to the drawing board. Amit notes his Seen and the Unseen guests made the counterintuitive case that nuclear weapons make conventional war more important.
core_ideas.quote: No, conventional war is back. Conventional war remains important and we need to figure this out.

core_ideas.concept: Small, Cheap and Civilian Beats Exquisite Platforms
core_ideas.explanation:
Ajay's prescriptions for procurement:
- Use commercial off-the-shelf technology wherever possible. Starlink, a mass-market product, has huge military value, and a battlefield 3D printer should be an ordinary civilian one.
- Question big showpiece platforms. Shore-based missiles on Great Nicobar could dominate the Straits of Malacca, which raises the question of whether carriers are needed there.
- Rebuild procurement for speed. Ukraine fields a new generation of drones every four months, so aim for three revisions a year rather than one every five years.
core_ideas.quote: We've got to get out of the Raytheon and McDonnell Douglas kind of vendors and 30-year equipment cycles into far more Silicon Valley type, small, fast, nimble, you know, get things done the DARPA way

core_ideas.concept: All Roads Lead to Scale, and Hence to Partnership
core_ideas.explanation: Military production follows Wright's Law: costs fall only with volume. Only the US and China have budgets large enough to reach scale alone; everyone else going it alone ends up subscale, expensive and short on R&D. The way out is deep international collaboration, with five to ten countries buying the same gear. Ajay points to two 'vortexes': a post-Trump European defence industrial base, and a Poland-Ukraine-South Korea partnership aiming for lower price points. India could manufacture for the latter, since a factory in Tamil Nadu is far from any front. Ajay cites India's Israel partnership since Narasimha Rao's time, which upgraded old Soviet equipment cheaply, as proof this works.
core_ideas.quote: So from all these points of view, all roads lead to scale. The most fundamental idea in defense economics is scale.

core_ideas.explanation: Ukraine's flood of innovation reflects incentives, since it is fighting for its life, but also freedom. Free citizens bring their whole selves to the effort, while subjects of authoritarian states merely obey and become shadows of themselves. Amit frames it as citizen versus subject: citizens have skin in the game.
core_ideas.quote: Authoritarians are just not able to harness their people. Freedom works.

core_ideas.concept: Speed, Autonomy and the Need for New Doctrine
core_ideas.explanation: Edge AI lets drones pick and strike targets without a human in the loop. Ajay calls this ethically fraught but inevitable, since countries like Russia and China won't sign treaties against it. Amit fears that the incentive for speed will push decisions to machines, and mistakes at scale could be catastrophic. Ajay's response is to do for conventional war what von Neumann, Nash and Schelling did for nuclear weapons after 1945: build game-theoretic deterrence doctrines that make for stable, peaceful behaviour.
core_ideas.quote: What if the last human decision in a war is a decision to start the war?

core_ideas.concept: The New Fog of War: Are We at War, and With Whom?
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's second fear is ambiguity on two fronts. A power outage, a GST or Aadhaar backend failure, or contaminated water could be an accident, terrorism or a deliberate act of war. Cheap drones mean the attacker could be Pakistan, China, a dissident group, internal actors or the state's own false flag. In that fog, societies are liable to panic and make mistakes.
core_ideas.quote: you don't know what is war and what is not. That's number one. And number two is you don't know who's waging it.

core_ideas.concept: Make Trade, Not War: Be Citizens, Not Subjects
core_ideas.explanation: Geopolitics often runs on a zero-sum, mercantilist instinct that makes war seem natural. But human flourishing has always come through trade and peaceful cooperation. India should trade with China and Pakistan, and musicians on both sides should keep jamming. Amit's exhortation is to act as citizens: demand a state ready for future war, but one that actively makes peace rather than mongering war. Ajay agrees, adding that there is evil in the world, so the state still needs capabilities.
core_ideas.quote: War helps no one, it's a terrible negative sum game.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit says Ajay's pitch for a future-of-war episode felt like 'a glitch in the matrix, in other words, Deja Vu', since they'd already covered hybrid warfare and the world in 2050. He adds: 'We are not like other YouTube channels that we will recycle our old material and repeat ourselves as you know, men with egos tend to do. Shameful. Absolutely shameful.'

Amit on why Ukraine innovates so furiously: 'when you have a breakfast of bacon and eggs, what is the difference between the chicken and the pig? And the answer is that the chicken is interested, but the pig is committed. And in that sense, Ukraine is a pig.'
A riddle on incentives: 'Who runs faster, the fox or the hare?' The punchline: 'The fox is only running for his lunch. The hare is running for his life.'

Ajay on a Russian helicopter hunting a Ukrainian drone boat: 'Just think of the arrogance and the confidence of a helicopter. You feel you are the god of the sky, and you're looking down at a dumb boat... and the boat says, Oops, and it just puts up its hand and a missile flies out of the boat and shoots down a helicopter.'

Ajay describes the relative calm of a First World War trench: 'You're talking to your buddies. You're drinking water.' Amit chips in: 'You're writing diary entries about masturbation, as Wittgenstein did, the great philosopher.'

Ajay's test for listeners: 'put on your sorting hat and classify yourself that are you a genuine military geek or are you fake? A genuine military geek knows the names of all the operations.' He lists Barbarossa, Citadel and Market Garden, and says Operation Spider Web will join them in history.
On the false ceilings that hid the Spider Web drones, Ajay notes you only need about six inches. Amit: 'You just need six inches, that's what she said.'

Amit, having established that Ajay is no expert on Indian mass culture, asks a quiz anyway: 'if the famous nineteen seventies actor Ajit was to take part in an uprising, what would that uprising be called? Operation Rising Loin.'
As Ajay scales drone swarms from ten to a hundred to 10,000, Amit quips: 'You just change the kitty party into a cricket match.'

Ajay's friend Ayush Patnaik built a 3D printer that prints everything about itself except one nozzle: 'you have to buy one nozzle and then you have to give Ayush one milk shake and he will print a three D printer for you.' Amit extrapolates that with some AGI, aliens landing on Earth 'will think that the dominant species here are these three D printers. And us humans there'll be some fossils around.' Ajay tops it: 'There is another amazing pathway to a 3D printer which is called a woman.'

Amit sets up the principles chapter by imagining 'the grand leader of this country comes to you, a fellow Gujarati'. The leader asks Ajay to revamp the military and makes a second request: 'can your friend Ayush give me a three D printer like this, I will buy him a milkshake.'
After a long stretch on Tiger and King Tiger tanks, Ajay announces 'I want to digress.' Amit: 'You were talking tiger tanks. We can get you a tigress.'

Ajay says the military needs 'wimps like Vaishnav'. Amit leaps to his friend's defence, Ajay clarifies he wants 'Vaishnav levels of genius', Amit adds 'And the lack of biceps', and Ajay replies that 'biceps are fully trainable'. Amit closes: 'please do not mess with my friends... I will wage war against you.'

Ajay on his organisation: 'in my organization, XKDR Forum, we are crazy geeks. We in addition to loving FDI and loving our programming, we also love government contracting. We think government contracting is hot.'

How this episode came about: Amit emailed 'history of war', Ajay replied 'future of war', Amit repeated 'history of war', Ajay repeated 'future of war', until Amit realised Ajay had a different idea. Ajay's justification: every child already knows 'everything that happened in the Second World War and Six Day War.'
Amit's sign-off: 'We hope none of our worst fears come true. And we trade and trade and trade until we can trade no more. Make trade, not war.'

D-Day, 6 June 1944: Normandy residents were woken around 3 am by the drone of thousands of Allied planes flying for hours from Britain. Ajay says this is what thousand-strong drone swarms will look like.
The Spanish Civil War of 1936 as the lab 'where Adolf Hitler perfected the Blitzkrieg'. It is Ajay's analogy for why every military should study Ukraine up close.

Johnny von Neumann, John Nash and Thomas Schelling: after Hiroshima and Nagasaki they worked out game-theoretic nuclear doctrine. Ajay proposes similar thinking for conventional deterrence between India and China or India and Pakistan.

Israel's 1967 war, which people joke was Second World War capability fully realised, and the Gulf War as 'the first triumph of silicon over steel'. Ajay uses them as the last 'recognisable' wars before today's break.
Gandhi first met Gopal Krishna Gokhale in 1894 on the grounds of Fergusson College in Pune, where they took a walk together.
